title: French foundations
description: Twenty-four original A1 foundation lessons. A growing course, not a complete A1 certification syllabus. Now expanded with 18 CEFR A2 lessons in 5 new units — Le passé raconté, L’avenir et les projets, Politesse et hypothèses, Précision et liens, Il faut que… — covering the passé composé, the imparfait, the futur simple, the conditional, first steps into the subjunctive, the pronouns y and en, relative pronouns, and comparatives and superlatives.

units.title: Going further
units.objective: Discuss destinations, past actions and plans.

units.title: Time and the world around you
units.objective: Handle days, time, weather and market prices.

units.title: Santé et vie sociale
units.objective: Handle aches, the pharmacy, emergencies and invitations.

units.title: En action
units.objective: Use your French in new ways: build, decide, remember.

units.title: En mission
units.objective: Use your French in the wild: navigate Paris, survive a headache, and build perfectly agreeing sentences.

units.title: Le passé raconté
units.objective: Tell what happened: build the passé composé and the imparfait, choose between them, and tell your day in order.

units.title: L’avenir et les projets
units.objective: Talk about what’s coming: form the futur simple, use it for promises and predictions, and name your projects and resolutions.

units.title: Politesse et hypothèses
units.objective: Soften requests and open imaginary worlds: the conditional for politeness and wishes, plus si + imparfait.

units.title: Précision et liens
units.objective: Speak with precision: the pronouns y and en, the relatives qui/que/où, comparatives and superlatives.

units.title: Il faut que…
units.objective: Say what must be done: first steps into the subjunctive, the vocabulary of work, a hotel mission, and a review of A1.

concepts.title: Names and introductions
concepts.explanation: Je means I. Je suis is the I-form of être (to be). French normally keeps the subject pronoun. Bonjour is a polite greeting; salut is informal. Française describes a French woman; français describes a French man.
concepts.commonError: With je, être is suis.

concepts.title: People and être
concepts.explanation: Tu is informal singular you; elle is she; il is he. Être changes: je suis, tu es, il/elle est. Unlike Italian, French normally needs the subject before the verb. Est and et (and) are different words.
concepts.commonError: With tu, use es. Est belongs with il or elle.

concepts.title: Family and avoir
concepts.explanation: Avoir means to have: j’ai, tu as, il/elle a. Je becomes j’ before ai; keep the apostrophe. Un frère uses a masculine article; une sœur is feminine. Learn the article with each noun.
concepts.commonError: Je contracts before ai: j’ai.

concepts.title: Numbers and age
concepts.explanation: French uses avoir for age: j’ai vingt ans literally means I have twenty years. Vingt means twenty and trente means thirty. Ans is years when counting age. Do not use être for a person’s age.
concepts.commonError: Use avoir for age: J’ai vingt ans.

concepts.title: Home and articles
concepts.explanation: Le is a masculine definite article and la is feminine. Both become l’ before a vowel sound. Une maison is a house; le livre is the book. À la maison means at home. The accent on à distinguishes it from a (has).

examples.target: Le livre est à la maison.

concepts.commonError: The book is masculine: le livre. La livre is a different noun meaning the pound.

concepts.title: Describing things
concepts.explanation: Many feminine adjectives add -e, but some change more: blanc → blanche. A white house is une maison blanche; a white book is un livre blanc. Grand becomes grande with a feminine noun.
concepts.commonError: Maison is feminine: use blanche.

concepts.title: Plural nouns and adjectives
concepts.explanation: Most French nouns and adjectives add -s in the plural. The definite article becomes les for both genders. The verb être becomes sont with plural third-person subjects. Many final s letters are silent, but matter in writing.
concepts.commonError: A plural subject needs sont.

concepts.title: Study and work
concepts.explanation: Regular -er verbs use -e with je and -es with tu: travailler → je travaille, tu travailles. Étudier begins with a vowel sound, so je becomes j’: j’étudie. French uses this present tense for both I study and I am studying.
concepts.commonError: The tu form of travailler ends in -es: travailles.

concepts.title: Making a negative
concepts.explanation: In careful written French, put ne before the verb and pas after it. Ne becomes n’ before a vowel: je n’étudie pas. Spoken French often omits ne, but this lesson practises the complete written form.

examples.target: Je n’étudie pas à la maison.
examples.meaning: I do not study at home.

concepts.commonError: Put the finite verb between ne and pas: Je ne travaille pas.

concepts.title: Asking simple questions
concepts.explanation: Est-ce que introduces a yes/no question without changing subject-verb order: Est-ce que tu travailles ? You can also ask Tu travailles ? with rising intonation. Qui asks who. This lesson uses the est-ce que frame.

examples.target: Est-ce que tu étudies à la maison ?

concepts.commonError: Keep the tu ending -es: tu travailles.

concepts.title: Ordering and prendre
concepts.explanation: Prendre is irregular: je prends, tu prends. In a café, je prends un café can mean I will have a coffee. Un thé is a tea. Keep the accents in café and thé. Je voudrais is a polite fixed frame meaning I would like.
concepts.commonError: With je, prendre is prends, including the final s.

concepts.title: Possession and agreement
concepts.explanation: Mon and ma mean my; they agree with the thing owned, not the owner. Use mon livre and ma maison. French does not put le or la before these possessives. Mes is plural for either gender.
concepts.commonError: Maison is feminine and begins with a consonant: ma maison.

concepts.title: Going places with aller
concepts.explanation: Aller is irregular: je vais, tu vas. À introduces destinations. À + le contracts to au; à la stays separate. Use à Paris with a city. À la gare means to the station.

examples.meaning: I am going to the station.

concepts.commonError: With je, aller is vais.

concepts.title: Can I? Modal requests
concepts.explanation: Pouvoir means can or be able to: je peux, tu peux. After it, use the infinitive: je peux prendre. Do not conjugate both verbs. Est-ce que makes the request a question. S’il vous plaît adds politeness.

examples.target: Est-ce que je peux prendre un café ?
Tu peux étudier à la maison.

concepts.commonError: After peux, use the infinitive prendre.

concepts.title: A first look at passé composé
concepts.explanation: The passé composé joins an auxiliary with a past participle. With étudier, use avoir: j’ai étudié. Regular -er participles end in -é. Hier means yesterday. This lesson introduces only avoir with the I-form; other auxiliaries come later.
concepts.commonError: Étudier uses avoir here: j’ai étudié.

concepts.title: Near-future plans
concepts.explanation: French often expresses a plan with aller + infinitive: je vais étudier means I am going to study. Keep vais conjugated, and leave étudier in the infinitive. Demain means tomorrow. This differs from je vais à Paris, which names a destination.

examples.meaning: Tomorrow I am going to study.

examples.target: Tu vas travailler à la maison.
examples.meaning: You are going to work at home.

concepts.commonError: After vais for a plan, keep the infinitive étudier.

concepts.title: Days and dates
concepts.explanation: French days and months are masculine and written lowercase: lundi, mai. Give the date with le, the number and the month: le trois mai. Aujourd’hui, demain and hier frame any plan.
concepts.commonError: Days of the week are lowercase in French: lundi.

concepts.title: Telling the time
concepts.explanation: Ask the time with Quelle heure est-il ? Answer Il est une heure for one o’clock and Il est plus the number plus heures otherwise: Il est trois heures. Add et demie for half past, et quart for quarter past and moins le quart for quarter to.

examples.target: Il est trois heures et demie.

concepts.commonError: The clock always takes il est, singular or plural: Il est trois heures.

concepts.title: Weather and seasons
concepts.explanation: Describe the weather with il fait plus an adjective: il fait chaud for hot, il fait froid for cold. Say il y a du soleil for sunny and il pleut for it rains. Two seasons to know now are l’été (summer, masculine) and l’hiver (winter, masculine).
concepts.commonError: Weather uses faire, not être: Aujourd’hui, il fait froid.

concepts.title: Market prices
concepts.explanation: Ask the price with Combien coûte ? for one thing and Combien coûtent ? for several: Combien coûte un kilo de pommes ? Answer with the price: Ça fait trois euros. Un kilo is one kilo and le marché is the market.

examples.target: Combien coûte un kilo de pommes ?
examples.meaning: How much is a kilo of apples?

concepts.commonError: Un kilo is singular, so the question is singular: Combien coûte un kilo de pommes ?

concepts.title: Saying where it hurts
concepts.explanation: Say pain with J’ai mal plus the body part: J’ai mal à la tête. Headache is le mal de tête and fever is la fièvre. Answer Où avez-vous mal? (Where does it hurt?) with J’ai mal plus the spot.
concepts.commonError: Pain uses avoir mal, not être: J’ai mal à la tête.

concepts.title: Asking for medicine
concepts.explanation: Ask for medicine with Je voudrais…: Je voudrais un médicament. Un comprimé is a pill and le sirop is syrup. Ask the price with C’est combien ?: Ça coûte cinq euros.
concepts.commonError: Voudrais is polite: Je voudrais un médicament.

concepts.title: Calling for help
concepts.explanation: Call for help with Au secours ! Ask for an ambulance with Appelez une ambulance ! The emergency number is le cent-douze (112). Say C’est urgent when it is urgent.
concepts.commonError: Appelez is the polite command form: Appelez une ambulance !

concepts.title: Inviting and replying
concepts.explanation: Invite with Tu veux venir… ?: Tu veux venir dîner ? Accept with Oui, merci, avec plaisir. Decline politely with Désolé, je ne peux pas.

examples.meaning: Do you want to come to dinner Saturday?

concepts.commonError: Venir means to come: Tu veux venir dîner ?

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: French shares the Latin alphabet with English, and thousands of everyday words came into both languages from Latin — nation, information, restaurant, café. You can already recognize them before you speak a word of French. The words below are the first ones to say out loud: bonjour opens almost every conversation, merci answers kindness, oui and non steer it.
concepts.commonError: Say bonjour the moment you arrive — the French notice silence more than accent. Save bonsoir for the evening.

concepts.title: Commander et payer au café
concepts.explanation: Use Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît for a polite order. Ask Combien ça coûte ? for the price and say Merci.

examples.target: Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.

concepts.commonError: Je voudrais is the polite request form; keep s’il vous plaît with the request.

concepts.title: The passé composé with avoir
concepts.explanation: To talk about yesterday, French uses two beats: a helper verb (avoir, in the present) plus a past participle. J’ai mangé — literally “I have eaten” — is how French says “I ate”. The helper changes with the person (j’ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont); the participle stays still. For -er verbs the participle ends in -é: mangé, parlé, regardé. For -ir verbs it ends in -i: fini. Some are irregular and must be met one by one: prendre → pris.
concepts.commonError: Saying the participle alone (« mangé ») with no helper — the helper is what puts the action in the past. Always two beats: j’ai + mangé.

concepts.title: The imparfait
concepts.explanation: The imparfait describes what was happening, what used to happen, and how things were. Formation is beautifully regular: take the nous form of the present, drop -ons, and add -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Nous parlons → parl- → je parlais, tu parlais, il parlait, nous parlions, vous parliez, ils parlaient. One rebel: être does not use its nous form — it uses ét-: j’étais.

examples.meaning: I was speaking. / I used to speak.
Did you use to live in Paris ?

concepts.commonError: Using the infinitive as the stem (« je parlerais » is the conditional, not the imparfait). The stem comes from the nous present: parlons → parl-.

concepts.title: Two pasts, two jobs
concepts.explanation: The passé composé photographs one finished action: je suis entré — I came in, done. The imparfait paints the background: what was happening (il pleuvait), what used to happen (je marchais), how things were (j’avais dix ans). The classic scene: background in the imparfait, then a new event interrupts in the passé composé — je marchais quand le téléphone a sonné.
concepts.commonError: Putting every past action in the passé composé. Ask: is it a finished event (photo) or the background/scene (painting) ? Background, habits and descriptions take the imparfait.

concepts.title: Telling your day
concepts.explanation: A day told in order needs two tools: sequencing words (d’abord “first”, puis “then”, ensuite “next”, enfin “finally”) and the two pasts. The passé composé moves the story forward — je me suis levé, j’ai appelé. The imparfait sets each scene — il faisait beau. String them together and even simple words sound like a story.

examples.target: Ensuite, je suis allé au travail.

concepts.commonError: Telling events in a jumble with no sequencing words. French ears expect d’abord… puis… ensuite… enfin — the skeleton of every “ma journée”.

concepts.title: The futur simple
concepts.explanation: The futur simple is one word: the infinitive plus an ending — -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Je parlerai, tu parleras, il parlera, nous parlerons, vous parlerez, ils parleront. The endings sound like avoir (ai, as, a, avons…) because historically they are: the future grew out of “to have”. Some verbs have irregular stems you meet one by one: être → ser- (je serai), avoir → aur-, aller → ir-, faire → fer-.
concepts.commonError: Using the present for a real future (« je travaille demain » works for plans, but promises and predictions want the futur simple: je travaillerai).

concepts.title: Near future vs simple future
concepts.explanation: French has two futures for two distances. The futur proche — aller in the present + infinitive (je vais manger) — is for what’s near and already decided: it’s in the diary. The futur simple (je mangerai) reaches further, or makes a promise, or predicts: it’s in the imagination. “Nous allons voyager” = the tickets are bought; “nous voyagerons” = the dream is alive.
concepts.commonError: Using the futur simple for something happening in five minutes that’s already arranged — French ears expect je vais le faire. Near + decided = futur proche.

concepts.title: Talking about projects
concepts.explanation: Projects need two kinds of language: naming the plan and committing to it. Avoir l’intention de (“to intend to”), décider de (“to decide to”) and espérer (“to hope to”) name the plan and take the infinitive: j’ai l’intention de lire. The futur simple seals it: je lirai. Plan in the infinitive, commitment in the future.
concepts.commonError: Putting a conjugated verb after décider de (« j’ai décidé je arrête »). After de, French wants the infinitive: j’ai décidé d’arrêter.

concepts.title: The conditional of politeness
concepts.explanation: The conditional softens everything into “would”. Formation: take the future stem (the infinitive, usually) and add the imparfait endings — -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Je parlerais, tu parlerais, il parlerait, nous parlerions, vous parleriez, ils parleraient. The workhorses of politeness: je voudrais (“I would like”), j’aimerais (“I would love”), pourriez-vous (“could you”), auriez-vous (“would you have”).
concepts.commonError: Using je veux (“I want”) for requests — grammatically fine, socially blunt. The conditional voudrais is the polite default.

concepts.title: The conditional of wishes
concepts.explanation: Same form as politeness, new job: the imagination. J’aimerais + infinitive or noun names what you dream of: j’aimerais voyager, j’aimerais un café. Je voudrais works the same way. The conditional keeps wishes soft and possible — it’s the difference between a demand and a dream.

examples.meaning: I would like to see the sea.

concepts.commonError: Saying wishes in the present (« je veux voyager ») — it sounds like a demand, not a dream. The conditional is what makes it a wish.

concepts.title: Si + imparfait → conditionnel
concepts.explanation: The great French “if”: si + imparfait sets an imaginary world, and the conditional lives in it. Si j’avais le temps, je voyagerais — “If I had time, I would travel.” The imparfait (j’avais) opens the hypothesis; the conditional (je voyagerais) is its consequence. The classic trap: never put the conditional after si itself. Si j’aurais is the famous mistake; si j’avais is the rule.

examples.target: Si j’avais le temps, je voyagerais.
examples.meaning: If I had time, I would travel.

examples.target: Si tu venais, je serais content.
examples.meaning: If you came, I would be happy.
If it rained, we would stay.

examples.target: Si j’étais riche, j’achèterais une maison.
examples.meaning: If I were rich, I would buy a house.

concepts.commonError: Putting the conditional after si (« si j’aurais ») — the most famous French mistake. After si, the imparfait: si j’avais.

concepts.title: Y and en
concepts.explanation: Two tiny pronouns do huge work. Y replaces à + a place or thing: je vais au café → j’y vais (“I’m going there”). En replaces de + a thing, or a quantity: tu veux du gâteau ? → j’en veux (“I want some”); il a deux sœurs → il en a deux (“he has two of them”). Both slide in before the verb — j’y pense, tu en veux — and both make you sound instantly fluent.
concepts.commonError: Repeating the noun (« je vais au café » every time) or putting y/en after the verb. They go before: j’y vais, j’en veux.

concepts.title: Qui, que, où
concepts.explanation: To link two ideas, French uses three small words. Qui = who/which when it’s the subject doing the verb: le collègue qui m’aide (“the colleague who helps me”). Que = whom/which when the verb acts on it: le rapport que j’écris (“the report I’m writing”). Où = where — and also when: le bureau où je travaille, le jour où je suis né.

examples.target: Le jour où je suis né.

concepts.commonError: Using que for everything (« le collègue que m’aide »). Ask: does the word after do the verb (qui) or receive it (que) ?

concepts.title: Comparatives
concepts.explanation: Comparing is a sandwich: plus + adjective + que (“more … than”), moins + adjective + que (“less … than”), aussi + adjective + que (“as … as”). Paris est plus grand que Lyon. The adjective still agrees with what it describes: elle est plus grande. One rebel: bon (“good”) becomes meilleur (“better”) — never “plus bon”.

examples.target: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

concepts.commonError: Saying « plus bon » — bon is irregular and becomes meilleur. Also forgetting that the adjective still agrees: plus grande, plus rapides.

concepts.title: Superlatives
concepts.explanation: The superlative crowns the comparison: le/la/les + plus/moins + adjective (+ de). C’est le plus grand — “it’s the biggest”. The article agrees with the noun (le plus grand, la plus belle, les moins chers), and the adjective agrees too. Two irregular crowns: bon → le meilleur (“the best”), mauvais → le pire (“the worst”).
concepts.commonError: Forgetting the article (« plus grand » alone is just a comparison). The superlative needs its crown: le plus grand, la moins chère.

concepts.title: Il faut que + subjunctive
concepts.explanation: After il faut que (“it’s necessary that”), French switches mood into the subjunctive. Il faut que tu viennes — “you must come”. Formation: take the ils form of the present, drop -ent, and add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent. Ils boivent → boiv- → que tu boives. For -er verbs it looks just like the present — the que after il faut is the signal that you’ve changed mood.

examples.target: Il faut que je me repose.
Il faut que tu boives de l’eau.

concepts.commonError: Using the infinitive after il faut que (« il faut que tu venir »). Il faut que opens a whole clause with a conjugated verb in the subjunctive: il faut que tu viennes.

concepts.title: The vocabulary of work
concepts.explanation: Work words unlock the fastest path to real French friendships: small talk with colleagues. Le bureau (“office”), le/la collègue (“colleague”), le patron (“boss”), le salaire (“salary”), la réunion (“meeting”), le congé (“leave, vacation”). Learn them as a set — they travel together in every office story.

examples.meaning: The boss is in a meeting.

concepts.commonError: Mixing up le patron (the boss, a person) with le bureau (the office, a place). People vs places — keep the set sorted.

concepts.title: Checking in at a hotel
concepts.explanation: A hotel check-in is a script with four lines: greet (bonsoir), state the booking (j’ai réservé une chambre), give the name (c’est au nom de…), and take the key (merci). Learn the lines and the night is yours. The receptionist’s questions — “c’est à quel nom ?”, “pour combien de nuits ?” — are the cues you listen for.

examples.meaning: Good evening, I booked a room.

concepts.commonError: Skipping the greeting and opening with the demand. In France the bonsoir comes first — always — or the script stalls.

stimuli.body:
Mission : un pique-nique samedi.
1. Va au marché.
2. Achète trois choses : un café, un thé, un kilo de pommes.
3. Invite un ami : « Tu veux venir samedi ? »
4. Annonce ton plan.
stimuli.translation: Mission: a picnic on Saturday. 1. Go to the market. 2. Buy three things: a coffee, a tea, a kilo of apples. 3. Invite a friend: “Do you want to come Saturday?” 4. Announce your plan.

stimuli.body:
Mission : un jour à Paris.
1. Va à la gare.
2. Trouve le marché : « Où est le marché ? »
3. Rentre à la maison à midi.
stimuli.translation: Mission: a day in Paris. 1. Go to the station. 2. Find the market: “Where is the market?” 3. Get home by midday.

stimuli.body:
Mission : à la pharmacie.
1. Dis où tu as mal : « J'ai mal à la tête. »
2. Va à la pharmacie.
3. Demande un médicament, s'il vous plaît.
4. Prends un comprimé ce soir.
stimuli.translation: Mission: to the pharmacy. 1. Say where it hurts: “My head hurts.” 2. Go to the pharmacy. 3. Ask for medicine, please. 4. Take a pill this evening.

stimuli.translation: Yesterday, I ate at the restaurant with Marie. We had the set menu. Did you finish your dessert ? Me, I finished everything !

stimuli.body: Construis des phrases comme un maçon : bloc par bloc. L'adjectif s'accorde avec le nom — blanc devient blanche avec « maison ». Assemble, vérifie, recommence.
Le pluriel, c'est de la construction : ajoute -s, change le en les, et n'oublie pas l'adjectif. Les blocs s'emboîtent — à toi de les assembler.
La négation, c'est un sandwich : ne devant le verbe, pas derrière. Ne devient n' devant une voyelle. Construis des phrases négatives, bloc par bloc.
Une question, ça se construit : est-ce que devant, et la phrase ne bouge pas. Qui et où ouvrent la question. Assemble des questions qui sonnent juste.
Mon, ma, mes : le possessif s'accorde avec l'objet possédé, pas avec le possesseur. Ma maison, mon livre. Construis — et choisis le bon bloc.
Souviens-toi : dans « Numbers and age », tu as appris à compter — et les dates sont des nombres déguisés. Le 3 mai, c'est « le trois mai ». Pas de nouvelle grammaire aujourd'hui : juste ta mémoire.
Souviens-toi : dans « Days, months and dates », tu as appris la semaine — lundi, vendredi, aujourd'hui, demain. L'heure, c'est un jour + un nombre. Ta mémoire a déjà tout.
Souviens-toi : dans « The future in one word », le futur simple tenait en une terminaison — -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Demain, bientôt : ta mémoire connaît déjà la musique.
Souviens-toi : dans « Near-future plans », tout projet commençait par aller + infinitif — « Demain, je vais étudier. » Aujourd'hui, ce soir, demain : ta mémoire sait déjà construire l'avenir proche.
Souviens-toi : dans « Study and work », tu as appris les verbes du quotidien — j'étudie, tu travailles, chaque jour. Le bureau d'aujourd'hui parle la langue d'hier.
Marie entre dans sa nouvelle maison. Elle est petite et blanche. Elle pose son livre sur la table, près de la porte. Mais son chat noir a disparu. « Minou ? » appelle Marie.
Le soir, Marie cherche son chat à la maison. Elle regarde sous la table et derrière la porte. Son livre est toujours sur la table. Puis elle entend un petit « miaou ».
Le chat dort sur le livre ! Marie rit : « Tu aimes mon livre ? » Ils ont enfin trouvé leur place dans la nouvelle maison.
Anna a bientôt un contrôle de français. Chaque jour, elle étudie à la maison : le matin, le français ; l'après-midi, les maths. Sur sa table, une note dit : « Une page à la fois. »
À midi, son ami Marc travaille à la maison, sur son ordinateur. Il apporte deux sandwichs. Anna ferme enfin son livre et ils mangent ensemble. « Tu travailles beaucoup ! » dit-elle.
Le soir, Anna finit ses maths. Elle sourit en regardant sa note : « Demain, je vais encore étudier le français. Après, je me repose ! »
Hier matin, Marc a étudié le français à la maison. Il a renversé son café sur ses notes, mais il a continué. « J'ai étudié ! » dit-il, fier.
L'après-midi, Anna a travaillé à la maison, sur son ordinateur. Marc a recopié ses notes. Puis ils ont mangé ensemble et ils ont ri des taches de café.
Le soir, Marc ferme enfin son livre. « Hier, j'ai étudié. Aujourd'hui, je me repose ! » Anna montre les pages tachées et rit encore.
Anna et Marc ont une journée chargée demain. Anna va étudier le français le matin et les maths l'après-midi. Elle accroche son plan au-dessus de sa table.
Marc va travailler à la maison. Ce soir, ils préparent les livres, l'ordinateur et le café. Mais le pot de café est vide.
Anna ajoute une dernière chose à leur liste : acheter du café demain matin. « Voilà notre plan ! » dit-elle.
Hier, je voulais raconter ma journée. D'abord, je me suis levé à sept heures. Puis j'ai pris mon téléphone. Ensuite, nous avons déjeuné ensemble.
L'après-midi, il faisait beau et nous avons marché. Sur le chemin du retour, mon téléphone est tombé : l'écran était cassé. Enfin, je suis rentré. Malgré tout, la journée était belle.
À la maison, j'écris quatre mots dans mon journal : d'abord, puis, ensuite, enfin. L'écran était cassé, mais ce n'était pas toute la journée.
Sur mon bureau, il y a un billet pour Rome — dans mon rêve. Je visiterais la ville, j'aimerais voir le Colisée et je voudrais manger des pâtes.
Mes amis arrivent dans mon rêve. Nous visiterions Paris aussi : tu rêverais de voyager et je rêverais avec toi. Puis le réveil sonne.
Au réveil, j'écris une phrase sur un papier : « J'aimerais visiter Rome. » Le rêve peut devenir un projet.
Mon ordinateur se bloque pendant que je travaille. Je regarde une carte au mur : si j'avais le temps, je voyagerais au Japon et à Rome. Mais le travail m'attend.
Je continue de rêver : si j'étais riche, j'achèterais une grande maison blanche avec un jardin. Puis l'écran clignote encore. D'abord, je réparerais mon ordinateur.
Je ferme la carte et j'écris deux projets : un rêve et une tâche. Le rêve commence par « Si j'avais le temps… » ; la tâche, par mon ordinateur.

activities.prompt: Build the sentence: My book is white.

activities.body: You already talk about today. To talk about yesterday, French adds a helper: avoir, then a past participle. J’ai mangé — literally “I have eaten” — is how French says “I ate”. Two beats every time: the helper, then the ending. Notice the helper changes with the person; the participle stays still.

activities.prompt: J’ai mangé une pizza. You know mangé comes from manger, “to eat”. Which word is the helper that puts it in the past ?
activities.feedback: ai is the present of avoir — the helper that carries the past. mangé is the participle, the word that names what happened. J’ is just “I”, une just “a”.

activities.prompt: Think: the helper for je is ai. Fini comes from finir. How do you say “I finished” ? Build it from the two beats — then write it.
activities.feedback: J’ai fini. Helper ai + participle fini — the same two beats as J’ai mangé.

activities.prompt: Elle a pris un café. “She had a coffee.” Which word is the helper here — the present-tense avoir doing the past-tense job ?
activities.feedback: a is avoir for elle/il — the helper. pris is the irregular participle of prendre; you will meet pris, mis, écrit and a few friends one by one. Elle just points at who.

activities.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “We watched a movie.”
activities.feedback: Nous avons regardé un film. Helper avons for nous, participle regardé — the pattern holds for every person.

activities.prompt: New verb, same beats: parler → parlé. Say “You (tu) spoke.”
activities.feedback: Tu as parlé. Helper as for tu, participle parlé — swap the verb, keep the two beats.

activities.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ mangé à midi.
activities.feedback: avons — the helper for nous. The participle mangé never moves; the helper does all the person-work.

activities.prompt: What did they have at the restaurant ? (Reading)
activities.feedback: Le menu du jour — “the menu of the day”, the fixed-price lunch. The rule you just built: helper + participle, in the wild.

activities.body: Yesterday’s tense photographed finished actions. The imparfait paints: what was happening, what you used to do, how things were. And its formation is almost insultingly regular — one stem from the nous present, six musical endings. Notice how je parlais and tu parlais sound the same: French music over French spelling.

activities.prompt: Nous parlions. “We were speaking.” Which part is the new imparfait ending ?
activities.feedback: ‑ions is the nous ending of the imparfait — the stem parl- comes from parlons minus -ons. Nous just points at who; -ions does the time-work.

activities.prompt: Think: stem = nous form minus -ons. Nous finissons → stem finiss-. How do you say “I was finishing” ?
activities.feedback: Je finissais. Stem finiss- + -ais. Watch the double s — it comes from the nous form, not from nowhere.

activities.prompt: Il était malade. “He was sick.” Which verb breaks the nous-stem rule here ?
activities.feedback: était — être is the rebel. It uses the stem ét- instead of its nous form. Il just points; malade just describes.

activities.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “We used to live in Paris.”
activities.feedback: Nous habitions à Paris. Stem habit- from habitons, ending -ions for nous — the pattern you just derived.

activities.prompt: New verb: prendre, nous prenons → stem pren-. Say “They (ils) were taking.”
activities.feedback: Ils prenaient. Stem pren- + -aient for ils — same machine, new verb.

activities.prompt: Complete: Chaque été, nous ___ à la mer. (aller)
activities.feedback: allions — the imparfait of aller for nous. Chaque été (“every summer”) is the classic imparfait signal: a repeated past.

activities.body: You now own two pasts. The question is when to use which. Think of the passé composé as a photograph — one finished action, click — and the imparfait as a painting — the scene, the weather, what was going on. Notice the classic move: the painting first, then the photograph interrupts it.

activities.prompt: Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti. Two pasts in one sentence. Which one paints the background weather ?
activities.feedback: pleuvait — the imparfait paints the ongoing weather. suis sorti is the finished event that steps into the scene. quand (“when”) is just the hinge.

activities.prompt: Think: background = imparfait, new event = passé composé. The phone ringing is the new event. How do you say “The phone rang” ?
activities.feedback: Le téléphone a sonné. One finished event → photograph → passé composé: helper a + participle sonné.

activities.prompt: Je marchais quand le téléphone a sonné. Which verb is the interrupting event ?
activities.feedback: a sonné — the passé composé breaks into the imparfait background. marchais paints what was already happening; quand is the hinge again.

activities.prompt: Background habit now: “We used to eat at noon.” (manger)
activities.feedback: Nous mangions à midi. A repeated past — no single event — so the imparfait paints it: mangions.

activities.prompt: Complete: Soudain, il ___ mal à la tête. (avoir, passé composé)
activities.feedback: a eu — soudain (“suddenly”) marks a finished event, so photograph it: helper a + participle eu.

activities.prompt: Who wanted to see him ? (Reading)
activities.feedback: Le médecin — “the doctor”. C’était paints the background (imparfait of être); voulait paints the ongoing wish.

activities.prompt: D’abord, je me suis levé. Which word orders the story — “first” ?
activities.feedback: D’abord — the sequencing word. me suis levé is the passé composé of se lever (reflexive verbs take être); je just points at who.

activities.prompt: L’après-midi, il faisait beau et nous avons marché. Which verb sets the scene ?
activities.feedback: faisait — the imparfait paints the afternoon weather. avons marché is the finished event inside that scene; l’après-midi is just the time-frame.

activities.prompt: Complete: ___ je me suis levé à sept heures. (first)
activities.feedback: D’abord — the story has to start somewhere, and d’abord is the classic opening beat.

segments.text: je me suis levé à sept heures.

activities.body: One word can hold tomorrow. The futur simple takes the infinitive — the whole verb, untouched — and adds an ending: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Notice the endings sound like avoir. That’s no accident: the future tense literally grew out of “to have”.

activities.prompt: Je parlerai demain. Which ending says “I will” ?
activities.feedback: -ai is the je ending of the future — same letters as avoir’s ai, and that’s the history showing through. parler- is the untouched infinitive; demain just points at when.

activities.prompt: Think: infinitive + ending. Finir + -as = ? Say “You will finish.”
activities.feedback: Tu finiras. Infinitive finir, ending -as for tu — one word, no helper.

activities.prompt: Nous mangerons ensemble. Which ending is “we will” ?
activities.feedback: -ons — the nous ending, echoing avons. manger- is the infinitive stem; ensemble (“together”) is just company.

activities.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “She will take the train.”
activities.feedback: Elle prendra le train. prendre → prendr- + -a for elle/il — the final -e of the infinitive drops before the future ending.

activities.prompt: Irregular stem: être → ser-. Say “I will be there.”
activities.feedback: Je serai là. The rebel stem ser- + the regular ending -ai. Irregular stems, regular endings — that’s the whole deal.

activities.prompt: Complete: Demain, tu ___ à la maison. (travailler)
activities.feedback: travailleras — infinitive + -as for tu. Demain points at the future; the ending does the work.

activities.prompt: When will the meeting start ? (Reading)
activities.feedback: À dix heures — “at ten”. commencera is the future doing its job in the wild.

activities.prompt: Je vais manger. Which two words build the near future ?
activities.feedback: vais manger — aller in the present + the infinitive. That’s the whole machine: near + decided. Je just points at who.

activities.prompt: Think: a promise takes the futur simple. “I will call you” (appeler).
activities.feedback: Je t’appellerai. A promise → futur simple. And watch the spelling: appeler doubles its l for je/tu/il (appellerai) but not for nous/vous (appellerons).

activities.prompt: Il fera beau. “The weather will be nice.” Which verb has an irregular future stem ?
activities.feedback: fera — faire → fer- is an irregular stem, with the regular ending -a. Il is just the weather’s dummy subject; beau just describes.

activities.prompt: Prediction now: “It will rain tomorrow.” (pleuvoir)
activities.feedback: Il pleuvra demain. A prediction → futur simple: pleuvr- + -a. Demain could also open the sentence — French is flexible with time words.

activities.prompt: Complete: Tu ___ : c’est une promesse. (réussir)
activities.feedback: réussiras — a promise lives in the futur simple: infinitive + -as.

activities.prompt: J’ai l’intention de lire. Which chunk names the plan — “intend” ?
activities.feedback: l’intention de — the plan-word. J’ai (“I have”) just carries it; lire is the infinitive it opens the door to.

activities.prompt: Think: décider de + infinitif. “I decided to stop.”
activities.feedback: J’ai décidé d’arrêter. décider de demands the infinitive — d’arrêter, with élision before the vowel.

activities.prompt: J’espère réussir. After espérer, what form follows ?
activities.feedback: réussir — the infinitive, as always after a plan-word. J’ points at who; espère names the hope.

activities.prompt: Commit it: “I will sleep eight hours.”
activities.feedback: Je dormirai huit heures. Infinitive dormir + -ai — the future sealing the resolution.

activities.prompt: Complete: J’ai ___ de changer. (décider, passé composé)
activities.feedback: décidé — the decision already happened, so photograph it: helper ai + participle décidé.

activities.body: One ending changes everything about how you sound. The conditional turns “I want” into “I would like” and “can you” into “could you”. Formation is a handshake between two tenses you know: the future stem plus the imparfait endings. Notice how every request in the examples melts a little.

activities.prompt: Je voudrais un café. Which word softens the request — “would like” ?
activities.feedback: voudrais — the conditional of vouloir. Je points at who; un café is just what’s wanted.

activities.prompt: Think: future stem of pouvoir is pourr- + conditional ending. “Could you help me ?” (vous)
activities.feedback: Pourriez-vous m’aider ? Stem pourr- + -iez for vous, and the pronoun flips after the verb in the question — the full polite package.

activities.prompt: J’aimerais réserver. Which ending marks the conditional here ?
activities.feedback: -ais — the je/tu conditional ending on the future stem aimer-. J’ points at who; réserver is the infinitive it governs.

activities.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “Would you have a table ?”
activities.feedback: Auriez-vous une table ? Conditional of avoir (aur- + -iez) with inversion — the classic restaurant opening.

activities.prompt: Soften it further: “Could you show me ?” (vous)
activities.feedback: Pourriez-vous me montrer ? Same machine — pourr- + -iez — new infinitive. Politeness is a pattern, not a phrasebook.

activities.prompt: Complete: Je ___ une chambre calme. (vouloir, conditionnel)
activities.feedback: voudrais — the polite default for “I would like”. A blunt veux would still be understood, just less loved.

activities.prompt: How many nights ? (Reading)
activities.feedback: Deux nuits — “two nights”. The whole passage is a masterclass in soft requests: voudrais, auriez-vous, pourriez-vous.

activities.prompt: J’aimerais voyager. Which verb form carries the wish ?
activities.feedback: aimerais — the conditional of aimer. J’ points at who; voyager is the infinitive the wish governs.

activities.prompt: Je rêve de voyager. After rêver de, what form follows ?
activities.feedback: voyager — the infinitive, as always after de. Je points at the dreamer; rêve names the dreaming.

activities.prompt: Write in French: They would visit Rome.
activities.feedback: Ils visiteraient Rome. Stem visiter- + -aient for ils — same pattern, new dreamers.

activities.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ partir au Japon. (aimer, conditionnel)
activities.feedback: aimerions — the conditional for nous: stem + -ions. The wish belongs to “we” now.

activities.prompt: Si j’avais le temps, je voyagerais. Which clause sets the imaginary world ?
activities.feedback: Si j’avais le temps — the si + imparfait clause opens the hypothesis. je voyagerais is the consequence that lives inside it.

activities.prompt: Si j’étais riche… Which verb is in the imparfait after si ?
activities.feedback: j’étais — être’s rebel imparfait stem ét-, right where the rule says the imparfait goes. Si opens it; riche just describes.

activities.prompt: Write in French: If I were rich, I would buy a house.
activities.feedback: Si j’étais riche, j’achèterais une maison. The full machine: hypothesis in the imparfait, consequence in the conditional.

answers: Si j’étais riche, j’achèterais une maison.

activities.prompt: Complete: Si tu ___, je serais content. (venir, imparfait)
activities.feedback: venais — after si, always the imparfait. The conditional (serais) waits for the consequence clause.

activities.body: French hates repeating itself. Instead of saying “the café” four times, it says it once and then points: y for à + place/thing, en for de + thing or quantity. Notice both words are tiny, both sit right before the verb, and both replace a whole chunk of meaning.

activities.prompt: J’y vais — “I’m going there.” Which English word does y stand for ?
activities.feedback: there — y replaces à + the place (au café → y). Je points at who; vais is the verb y leans on.

activities.prompt: Think: en replaces de + thing. “Do you want some (cake) ?”
activities.feedback: Tu en veux ? en stands for “some (of the cake)” — de + thing, swallowed into one syllable before the verb.

activities.prompt: J’y pense souvent. Where does y sit ?
activities.feedback: before the verb — y and en always lean on the verb from the left: j’y pense, j’en veux. After the verb is the classic beginner tell.

activities.prompt: Replace the noun: “Je vais au café” → use y.
activities.feedback: J’y vais. au café collapses into y, before the verb. Say it out loud — it’s the sound of fluency.

activities.prompt: Complete: Tu veux du gâteau ? Oui, j’___ veux.
activities.feedback: en — du gâteau (de + thing) becomes en. One letter doing the work of three words.

segments.text: Tu veux du gâteau ? Oui, j’

activities.body: Short sentences are safe; linked sentences are French. Qui, que and où are the hinges: qui when the next word does the verb, que when it receives the verb, où for where — and, sneakily, for when. Notice each example answers a question: who helps ? what am I writing ? where do I work ?

activities.prompt: Le collègue qui m’aide. Qui links to the subject — who helps ?
activities.feedback: Le collègue — the colleague does the helping, so qui is the subject-link. m’ (“me”) receives the help; aide is the verb.

activities.prompt: Think: que = the verb acts on it. “The report that I’m writing.”
activities.feedback: Le rapport que j’écris. I do the writing, the report receives it — so que, not qui.

activities.prompt: Le jour où je suis né. What does où mark here ?
activities.feedback: a time — où covers when as well as where. Le jour is a moment, not a place, and où handles both.

activities.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “The office where I work.”
activities.feedback: Le bureau où je travaille. A place → où. The hinge sits between the noun and its clause.

activities.prompt: Link it: “The colleague who helps me is nice.”
activities.feedback: Le collègue qui m’aide est sympa. qui links the helper to the description — one flowing sentence instead of two short ones.

answers: Le collègue qui m’aide est sympa.

activities.prompt: Complete: Le rapport ___ j’écris est long.
activities.feedback: que — j’écris acts on the report, so it’s the object-link. If the report were doing the writing, it would be qui.

activities.prompt: What is in the office ? (Reading)
activities.feedback: Une grande fenêtre — “a big window”. où links the office to its description, exactly the pattern you just built.

activities.body: French debates run on comparisons, and the machine is simple: plus for more, moins for less, aussi for as — then the adjective, then que. Notice the adjective keeps agreeing with what it describes, and notice the one rebel hiding in the examples’ shadow: bon becomes meilleur.

activities.prompt: Paris est plus grand que Lyon. Which word starts the comparison — “more” ?
activities.feedback: plus — the “more” marker. grand is the adjective (agreeing with Paris, masculine); que is the “than” hinge; Lyon is just the rival.

activities.prompt: Think: moins + adjective + que. “The train is less expensive.”
activities.feedback: Le train est moins cher. moins opens it, cher describes the train, and que would introduce the rival if there were one.

activities.prompt: L’hôtel est aussi beau. Which comparison is this — more, less, or as ?
activities.feedback: as — aussi + adjective (+ que) means “as … as”. The que is implied here: as beautiful (as the other one).

activities.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “This flight is faster.”
activities.feedback: Ce vol est plus rapide. plus + rapide, agreeing with vol (masculine) — no que needed when there’s no rival named.

activities.prompt: Compare with a rival: “The plane is faster than the train.”
activities.feedback: L’avion est plus rapide que le train. The full sandwich: plus + adjective + que + rival.

answers: L’avion est plus rapide que le train.

activities.prompt: Complete: Le train est ___ confortable que l’avion.
activities.feedback: plus — the train wins this round. The sandwich needs its opener: plus/moins/aussi.

activities.body: Comparisons have winners, and French crowns them with an article: le plus grand, la moins chère. Notice the crown — le/la/les — is what turns “bigger” into “the biggest”. And notice the two irregular crowns you already half-know: le meilleur, le pire.

activities.prompt: C’est le plus grand. Which word makes it “the most” — the superlative marker ?
activities.feedback: plus — but it only becomes “the most” with its crown, le. C’est just presents; grand is the adjective.

activities.prompt: Think: la + moins + chère (feminine). “It’s the cheapest (hotel).”
activities.feedback: C’est la moins chère. Feminine crown la, moins for “least”, chère agreeing feminine — the whole agreement chain.

activities.prompt: Le meilleur restaurant. Why not “le plus bon” ?
activities.feedback: bon is irregular — it becomes meilleur. “le plus bon” is the mistake every learner makes once; now you’ll never make it.

options.text: bon is irregular — it becomes meilleur

activities.prompt: Crown it: “The most famous monument.”
activities.feedback: Le monument le plus célèbre. Note the word order: with a noun, the crown repeats after it — le monument le plus célèbre.

activities.prompt: Complete: C’est ___ restaurant de Paris. (good → best)
activities.feedback: le meilleur — bon’s irregular crown. “le plus bon” would betray you.

activities.prompt: What does the Louvre have ? (Reading)
activities.feedback: La plus belle collection — “the most beautiful collection”. The superlative doing its job in the wild.

activities.body: A new mood — not a new tense. After il faut que, French stops stating facts and starts expressing necessity, and the verb changes its clothes: the subjunctive. Notice that for most verbs it looks exactly like the present. The que is the signal; the verb just follows its ils-present stem.

activities.prompt: Il faut que tu viennes. Which chunk triggers the subjunctive — “it’s necessary that” ?
activities.feedback: Il faut que — the trigger. tu viennes is the subjunctive clause it opens; viennes looks like the present, but the que tells you it’s the new mood.

activities.prompt: Think: ils boivent → stem boiv- + -e. “You must drink water.”
activities.feedback: Il faut que tu boives de l’eau. Stem boiv- from the ils present, ending -e for tu — the subjunctive machine working.

answers: Il faut que tu boives de l’eau.

activities.prompt: Il faut qu’elle dorme. The verb after que looks like the present — but what tells you it’s the subjunctive ?
activities.feedback: the que after il faut — the trigger is the signal. dorme happens to look like the present; the mood comes from il faut que.

activities.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “I need to rest.”
activities.feedback: Il faut que je me repose. The trigger, then the subjunctive: ils se reposent → stem repos- + -e.

activities.prompt: Say it: “She must sleep eight hours.”
activities.feedback: Il faut qu’elle dorme huit heures. qu’elle with élision, then dorme — ils dorment → dorm- + -e.

answers: Il faut qu’elle dorme huit heures.

activities.prompt: Complete: Il faut que tu ___ ton médicament. (prendre)
activities.feedback: prennes — ils prennent → prenn- + -es for tu. The double n comes from the ils form, not from nowhere.

activities.prompt: Ma collègue est sympa. You know “sympa” means nice. Which word means “colleague” ?
activities.feedback: collègue — the person-word. Ma just says “my”; est just links; sympa just describes.

activities.prompt: Think: “The boss is in a meeting.”
activities.feedback: Le patron est en réunion. Two new words in one natural sentence — le patron, la réunion — the way colleagues actually talk.

activities.prompt: Je prends un congé en août. What does congé mean here ?
activities.feedback: a holiday/leave — prendre un congé is “to take time off”. August is the sacred month; now you know the word for it.

activities.prompt: Say: “The salary is fine.”
activities.feedback: Le salaire est correct. correct here means “fine, decent” — a very French understatement.

activities.prompt: Complete: Le ___ est souvent en réunion. (boss)
activities.feedback: patron — the person-word. If it were the place, it would be bureau.

activities.body: You push through the revolving door into the lobby. The receptionist looks up and smiles. A check-in is a script — four lines, and the night is yours. Notice the lines in the examples: greet first, always.

activities.prompt: The receptionist looks up. What leaves your mouth first ?
activities.feedback: Bonsoir, j’ai réservé une chambre. — the greeting opens every interaction in France; the booking comes with it. Merci comes later, au revoir at the very end.

activities.prompt: She nods and taps the keyboard. Now state the booking plainly: “I booked a room.”
activities.feedback: J’ai réservé une chambre. The passé composé does the work — the booking happened, it’s done, réserver → réservé.

activities.prompt: She slides something across the desk. Build: “Here is the key.”
activities.feedback: Voici la clé. Voici presents — “here is” — and la clé is what you’ve been waiting for.

activities.prompt: She points upstairs. Complete: La chambre est au ___ étage. (second)
activities.feedback: deuxième — “second”. au deuxième étage: à + le contracts to au, and deuxième is the ordinal you’ll use in every hotel.

activities.prompt: “Le petit-déjeuner est à huit heures.” What is she telling you ?
activities.feedback: Breakfast is at eight. petit-déjeuner is “little lunch” — the French morning meal. Dinner would be le dîner; checkout, le départ.

options.text: The room is on the eighth floor.

activities.prompt: Think: the street side might be noisy. Ask for a quiet room: “Do you have a quiet room ?”
activities.feedback: Avez-vous une chambre calme ? — the polite inversion you learned for requests, now earning its keep in the real world.

answers: Est-ce que vous avez une chambre calme ?

activities.prompt: Quick check before you head up — match each line to its meaning.
activities.feedback: Three for three. The script is yours now.

left.text: Le petit-déjeuner est à huit heures.

activities.prompt: Final line — say the whole check-in in one breath: “Good evening, I booked a room.”
activities.feedback: Bonsoir, j’ai réservé une chambre. Greeting first, booking second — the script, performed.

activities.body: No new grammar today. Every question below comes from your earliest lessons: introductions, negation, questions, numbers, polite requests, descriptions, and the passé composé. Retrieval is what makes memories stick — think before you answer.

activities.prompt: Tu es Marie. “You are Marie.” Which verb form says “are” ?
activities.feedback: es — être for tu. Tu points at who; Marie is just the name; es does all the verb-work.

activities.prompt: Make it negative. Complete: Je ___ parle pas français.
activities.feedback: ne — the first half of ne…pas, hugging the verb: je ne parle pas. The pas alone is only half the negation.

activities.prompt: Ask: “Where is the station ?”
activities.feedback: Où est la gare ? — the question word où you met in “Asking simple questions”, still doing its job.

activities.prompt: Build: “It is three o’clock.”
activities.feedback: Il est trois heures. The dummy il, the être you’ve known since day one, and the number.

activities.prompt: Yesterday again. Complete: Hier, j’___ mangé une pizza. (helper)
activities.feedback: ai — the helper for je, the two-beat past you built in unit 9. The participle mangé waits for its helper.

activities.prompt: At the café, which is the polite way to order ?
activities.feedback: Un café, s’il vous plaît. — the softener s’il vous plaît turns a demand into a request. “Je veux” is understood, just blunt.

activities.prompt: Say: “I don’t understand.”
activities.feedback: Je ne comprends pas. The full ne…pas frame around the verb — the complete negation, both halves.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct ?
activities.feedback: Elle est française. — être + feminine adjective with its -e. “français” would describe a man; word order never splits est from its adjective like that.

activities.prompt: Photograph or painting? Match each line to the job its past tense is doing.
activities.feedback: Four for four. The passé composé snaps the photo; the imparfait paints the room the photo was taken in.

activities.prompt: Tiny words, big job. Match each line to what y or en is standing in for.
activities.feedback: All four. Y swallows à plus a place or an idea; en swallows de plus a thing. That really is the whole trick.

activities.prompt: Crown each line. Match the French superlative to the quality it names.
activities.feedback: Four crowns placed. Le plus, le moins, le meilleur — the crown always agrees with its noun.

activities.body: Mission briefing — read it twice, then go. It's Saturday morning at the Bastille market. Your mission: buy drinks for two friends — a coffee for Marc, a tea for Anna. You have everything you need: greet with « Bonjour », order with « Je prends… », pay, and say « Merci ». Three phrases. One mission. The vendor is waiting.

activities.prompt: Le marchand sourit : « Bonjour ! » Que réponds-tu en premier ?
activities.feedback: Bonjour d'abord — toujours. In France the greeting opens every exchange; the order comes after.

activities.prompt: Le marchand tend le sac : « Ça fait deux euros. » Tu paies. Que dis-tu ?
activities.feedback: Merci, au revoir ! — the mission ends the French way: thanks, then goodbye.

activities.prompt: Mission accomplie. Écris ta commande complète en français, comme tu la dirais au marchand : un café pour Marc et un thé pour Anna.
activities.feedback: Je prends un café et un thé, s'il vous plaît. — mission accomplished.

answers: Je prends un café et un thé, s'il vous plaît.
Je prends un café et un thé.
Un café et un thé, s'il vous plaît.

activities.body: Mission briefing. It's 6pm at the Gare de Lyon and your train leaves in twenty minutes from platform 7. Your mission: buy a ticket, find your way through the station, and board the right train. With « aller » you can say it all: « Je vais à Paris. » Read the briefing, then move.

activities.prompt: Au guichet : « Bonjour, vous allez où ? » Que réponds-tu ?
activities.feedback: Je vais à Paris — je + vais for yourself; tu vas is for the other person.

activities.prompt: Dans le train, le contrôleur demande : « Votre billet, s'il vous plaît. » Tu le tends et tu dis…
activities.feedback: Voilà — “here it is”, then merci. Mission nearly complete.

activities.prompt: Le train démarre. Écris en français où tu vas, comme tu le dirais à ton voisin.
activities.feedback: Je vais à Paris. — bon voyage !

activities.body: Mission briefing. It's 11pm. Your friend Marc has fallen on the stairs and his leg hurts. Your mission: call for help, ask for an ambulance, and give the address — 12 rue de la Paix, Paris. The emergency number is le quinze (15). Stay calm: in French, urgency is short sentences said clearly.

activities.prompt: Marc est par terre. Quel est le premier mot qui sort ?
activities.feedback: Au secours ! — “Help!” always comes first. Everything else can wait.

activities.prompt: L'opératrice demande : « C'est urgent ? » Tu réponds…
activities.feedback: Oui, c'est urgent ! — clear and direct. In an emergency, clarity saves time.

activities.prompt: Donne l'adresse à l'opératrice, en français : 12 rue de la Paix, Paris.
activities.feedback: 12 rue de la Paix, Paris. — l'ambulance arrive. Mission accomplished.

answers: C'est le 12 rue de la Paix, à Paris.

lessons.title: Yesterday, in two beats
lessons.objective: Form the passé composé with avoir: helper + past participle, and use it for finished actions.

legacyExercises.prompt: J’ai mangé une pizza. You know mangé comes from manger, “to eat”. Which word is the helper that puts it in the past ?
legacyExercises.explanation: ai is the present of avoir — the helper that carries the past. mangé is the participle, the word that names what happened. J’ is just “I”, une just “a”.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: the helper for je is ai. Fini comes from finir. How do you say “I finished” ? Build it from the two beats — then write it.
legacyExercises.explanation: J’ai fini. Helper ai + participle fini — the same two beats as J’ai mangé.

legacyExercises.prompt: Elle a pris un café. “She had a coffee.” Which word is the helper here — the present-tense avoir doing the past-tense job ?
legacyExercises.explanation: a is avoir for elle/il — the helper. pris is the irregular participle of prendre; you will meet pris, mis, écrit and a few friends one by one. Elle just points at who.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “We watched a movie.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Nous avons regardé un film. Helper avons for nous, participle regardé — the pattern holds for every person.

legacyExercises.prompt: New verb, same beats: parler → parlé. Say “You (tu) spoke.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Tu as parlé. Helper as for tu, participle parlé — swap the verb, keep the two beats.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Nous ___ mangé à midi.
legacyExercises.explanation: avons — the helper for nous. The participle mangé never moves; the helper does all the person-work.

legacyExercises.prompt: What did they have at the restaurant ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Le menu du jour — “the menu of the day”, the fixed-price lunch. The rule you just built: helper + participle, in the wild.
legacyExercises.passage: Hier, j’ai mangé au restaurant avec Marie. Nous avons pris le menu du jour. Tu as fini ton dessert ? Moi, j’ai tout fini !
legacyExercises.translation: Yesterday, I ate at the restaurant with Marie. We had the set menu. Did you finish your dessert ? Me, I finished everything !

lessons.culturalNote: The passé composé is the everyday spoken past in France — in conversation, almost every finished action uses it, even where English would use the simple past. If you can say « j’ai mangé », you can already tell yesterday.

lessons.title: The tense of “used to”
lessons.objective: Form the imparfait: nous-present stem minus -ons, plus -ais/-ait/-ions/-iez/-aient.

legacyExercises.prompt: Nous parlions. “We were speaking.” Which part is the new imparfait ending ?
legacyExercises.explanation: ‑ions is the nous ending of the imparfait — the stem parl- comes from parlons minus -ons. Nous just points at who; -ions does the time-work.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: stem = nous form minus -ons. Nous finissons → stem finiss-. How do you say “I was finishing” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: Je finissais. Stem finiss- + -ais. Watch the double s — it comes from the nous form, not from nowhere.

legacyExercises.prompt: Il était malade. “He was sick.” Which verb breaks the nous-stem rule here ?
legacyExercises.explanation: était — être is the rebel. It uses the stem ét- instead of its nous form. Il just points; malade just describes.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “We used to live in Paris.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Nous habitions à Paris. Stem habit- from habitons, ending -ions for nous — the pattern you just derived.

legacyExercises.prompt: New verb: prendre, nous prenons → stem pren-. Say “They (ils) were taking.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Ils prenaient. Stem pren- + -aient for ils — same machine, new verb.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Chaque été, nous ___ à la mer. (aller)
legacyExercises.explanation: allions — the imparfait of aller for nous. Chaque été (“every summer”) is the classic imparfait signal: a repeated past.

legacyExercises.prompt: How long did they stay ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Deux semaines — “two weeks”. The imparfait restions paints the habit; the number makes it concrete.
legacyExercises.passage: Quand j’étais petit, nous allions à la mer chaque été. L’hôtel était petit mais la plage était magnifique. Nous restions deux semaines.
legacyExercises.translation: When I was little, we used to go to the sea every summer. The hotel was small but the beach was magnificent. We stayed two weeks.

lessons.culturalNote: The imparfait is the tense of nostalgia — Proust’s madeleine moment lives in it. French speakers use it to paint the past; the passé composé photographs it. One stem, musical endings, and you can describe whole childhoods.

lessons.title: Photograph or painting ?
lessons.objective: Choose between passé composé (finished event) and imparfait (background, habit, description).

legacyExercises.prompt: Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti. Two pasts in one sentence. Which one paints the background weather ?
legacyExercises.explanation: pleuvait — the imparfait paints the ongoing weather. suis sorti is the finished event that steps into the scene. quand (“when”) is just the hinge.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: background = imparfait, new event = passé composé. The phone ringing is the new event. How do you say “The phone rang” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: Le téléphone a sonné. One finished event → photograph → passé composé: helper a + participle sonné.

legacyExercises.prompt: Je marchais quand le téléphone a sonné. Which verb is the interrupting event ?
legacyExercises.explanation: a sonné — the passé composé breaks into the imparfait background. marchais paints what was already happening; quand is the hinge again.

answers: Je dormais quand elle est arrivée.
legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “I was sleeping when she arrived.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Je dormais quand elle est arrivée. Imparfait dormais for the background, passé composé est arrivée for the arrival — note the agreement with être: arrivée.

legacyExercises.prompt: Background habit now: “We used to eat at noon.” (manger)
legacyExercises.explanation: Nous mangions à midi. A repeated past — no single event — so the imparfait paints it: mangions.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Soudain, il ___ mal à la tête. (avoir, passé composé)
legacyExercises.explanation: a eu — soudain (“suddenly”) marks a finished event, so photograph it: helper a + participle eu.

legacyExercises.prompt: Who wanted to see him ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Le médecin — “the doctor”. C’était paints the background (imparfait of être); voulait paints the ongoing wish.
legacyExercises.passage: Hier, il pleuvait quand je suis sorti. Je marchais dans la rue quand soudain mon téléphone a sonné. C’était le médecin : il voulait me voir.
legacyExercises.translation: Yesterday, it was raining when I went out. I was walking in the street when suddenly my phone rang. It was the doctor: he wanted to see me.

lessons.culturalNote: French storytelling lives in this contrast — novels and dinner-table anecdotes alike switch between the two pasts. Master the switch and you sound like a raconteur, not a textbook.

lessons.title: Raconte : ta journée
lessons.objective: Follow a day from first event to last, using time words to retell it.
lessons.culturalNote: Raconter sa journée is a French ritual — at dinner, « alors, ta journée ? » expects a real story, ordered and vivid. Sequencing words are the social glue; a day told in order sounds fluent even with simple words.

lessons.title: The future in one word
lessons.objective: Form the futur simple: infinitive + -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.

legacyExercises.prompt: Je parlerai demain. Which ending says “I will” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: -ai is the je ending of the future — same letters as avoir’s ai, and that’s the history showing through. parler- is the untouched infinitive; demain just points at when.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: infinitive + ending. Finir + -as = ? Say “You will finish.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Tu finiras. Infinitive finir, ending -as for tu — one word, no helper.

legacyExercises.prompt: Nous mangerons ensemble. Which ending is “we will” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: -ons — the nous ending, echoing avons. manger- is the infinitive stem; ensemble (“together”) is just company.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “She will take the train.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Elle prendra le train. prendre → prendr- + -a for elle/il — the final -e of the infinitive drops before the future ending.

legacyExercises.prompt: Irregular stem: être → ser-. Say “I will be there.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Je serai là. The rebel stem ser- + the regular ending -ai. Irregular stems, regular endings — that’s the whole deal.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Demain, tu ___ à la maison. (travailler)
legacyExercises.explanation: travailleras — infinitive + -as for tu. Demain points at the future; the ending does the work.

legacyExercises.prompt: When will the meeting start ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: À dix heures — “at ten”. commencera is the future doing its job in the wild.
legacyExercises.passage: Demain, je travaillerai à la maison. La réunion commencera à dix heures et le patron arrivera à neuf heures. Nous finirons tôt, puis nous mangerons ensemble.
legacyExercises.translation: Tomorrow, I will work from home. The meeting will start at ten and the boss will arrive at nine. We will finish early, then we will eat together.

lessons.culturalNote: The French future is a promise tense — « je te rappellerai » seals it. Note: for near, already-decided plans, French often prefers the futur proche (je vais travailler); the futur simple reaches further, or sounds more formal.

lessons.title: Remember : the future in one word
lessons.objective: Retrieve what you learned in « The future in one word » — one ending, every verb.
lessons.culturalNote: Weather forecasts live in the futur simple — « il pleuvra demain » — and so do New Year’s promises. The near future is for the diary; the simple future is for the imagination.

lessons.title: Remember : near-future plans
lessons.objective: Retrieve what you learned in « Near-future plans » — aller + infinitif, still the engine of every project.

lessons.title: The grammar of politeness
lessons.objective: Form the conditional (future stem + imparfait endings) and use je voudrais / pourriez-vous for soft requests.

legacyExercises.prompt: Je voudrais un café. Which word softens the request — “would like” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: voudrais — the conditional of vouloir. Je points at who; un café is just what’s wanted.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: future stem of pouvoir is pourr- + conditional ending. “Could you help me ?” (vous)
legacyExercises.explanation: Pourriez-vous m’aider ? Stem pourr- + -iez for vous, and the pronoun flips after the verb in the question — the full polite package.

legacyExercises.prompt: J’aimerais réserver. Which ending marks the conditional here ?
legacyExercises.explanation: -ais — the je/tu conditional ending on the future stem aimer-. J’ points at who; réserver is the infinitive it governs.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “Would you have a table ?”
legacyExercises.explanation: Auriez-vous une table ? Conditional of avoir (aur- + -iez) with inversion — the classic restaurant opening.

legacyExercises.prompt: Soften it further: “Could you show me ?” (vous)
legacyExercises.explanation: Pourriez-vous me montrer ? Same machine — pourr- + -iez — new infinitive. Politeness is a pattern, not a phrasebook.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Je ___ une chambre calme. (vouloir, conditionnel)
legacyExercises.explanation: voudrais — the polite default for “I would like”. A blunt veux would still be understood, just less loved.

legacyExercises.prompt: How many nights ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Deux nuits — “two nights”. The whole passage is a masterclass in soft requests: voudrais, auriez-vous, pourriez-vous.
legacyExercises.passage: Excusez-moi de vous déranger. Je voudrais réserver une chambre pour deux nuits. Auriez-vous une chambre calme ? Pourriez-vous me montrer le petit-déjeuner ? Merci beaucoup.
legacyExercises.translation: Sorry to disturb you. I would like to book a room for two nights. Would you have a quiet room ? Could you show me breakfast ? Thank you very much.

lessons.culturalNote: In France, politeness is grammar. « Je veux » at a counter sounds like a demand; « je voudrais » sounds like civilization. The conditional is the difference between being served and being stared at.

lessons.title: Histoire : le rêve
