lessons.culturalNote: J’aimerais is the French bucket-list verb — travel dreams, career dreams, dessert dreams. Saying a wish in the conditional keeps it deliciously possible, never demanding.

lessons.title: Histoire : si seulement…
lessons.objective: See how an everyday problem turns into two imaginary plans with si.
lessons.culturalNote: Si + imparfait is the French daydream machine — lunch-break conversations run on it. « Si j’avais le temps… » can open any fantasy. Master the pattern and you can imagine anything, grammatically.

lessons.title: The tiny words y and en
lessons.objective: Replace à + place/thing with y and de + thing/quantity with en, placed before the verb.

legacyExercises.prompt: J’y vais — “I’m going there.” Which English word does y stand for ?
legacyExercises.explanation: there — y replaces à + the place (au café → y). Je points at who; vais is the verb y leans on.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: en replaces de + thing. “Do you want some (cake) ?”
legacyExercises.explanation: Tu en veux ? en stands for “some (of the cake)” — de + thing, swallowed into one syllable before the verb.

legacyExercises.prompt: J’y pense souvent. Where does y sit ?
legacyExercises.explanation: before the verb — y and en always lean on the verb from the left: j’y pense, j’en veux. After the verb is the classic beginner tell.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “He has two (of them).”
legacyExercises.explanation: Il en a deux. en replaces “of them” — the quantity’s de — and sits before a.

legacyExercises.prompt: Replace the noun: “Je vais au café” → use y.
legacyExercises.explanation: J’y vais. au café collapses into y, before the verb. Say it out loud — it’s the sound of fluency.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Tu veux du gâteau ? Oui, j’___ veux.
legacyExercises.explanation: en — du gâteau (de + thing) becomes en. One letter doing the work of three words.

legacyExercises.prompt: What does he think about often ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Le café — “the café”. J’y pense points back to it without repeating it: that’s the whole lesson in one sentence.
legacyExercises.passage: Tu vas au café ? J’y vais aussi ! Tu veux du gâteau ? J’en veux bien. J’y pense souvent, à ce café. Il est parfait.
legacyExercises.translation: Are you going to the café ? I’m going there too ! Do you want some cake ? I’d like some. I think about it often, that café. It’s perfect.

lessons.culturalNote: Y and en are the sound of natural French — without them you repeat nouns like a robot (« je vais au café, je pense au café »). With them, you glide. French ears notice instantly.

lessons.title: Linking ideas: qui, que, où
lessons.objective: Link clauses with qui (subject), que (object), où (place/time).

legacyExercises.prompt: Le collègue qui m’aide. Qui links to the subject — who helps ?
legacyExercises.explanation: Le collègue — the colleague does the helping, so qui is the subject-link. m’ (“me”) receives the help; aide is the verb.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: que = the verb acts on it. “The report that I’m writing.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Le rapport que j’écris. I do the writing, the report receives it — so que, not qui.

legacyExercises.prompt: Le jour où je suis né. What does où mark here ?
legacyExercises.explanation: a time — où covers when as well as where. Le jour is a moment, not a place, and où handles both.

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “The office where I work.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Le bureau où je travaille. A place → où. The hinge sits between the noun and its clause.

answers: Le collègue qui m’aide est sympa.
legacyExercises.prompt: Link it: “The colleague who helps me is nice.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Le collègue qui m’aide est sympa. qui links the helper to the description — one flowing sentence instead of two short ones.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Le rapport ___ j’écris est long.
legacyExercises.explanation: que — j’écris acts on the report, so it’s the object-link. If the report were doing the writing, it would be qui.

legacyExercises.prompt: What is in the office ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Une grande fenêtre — “a big window”. où links the office to its description, exactly the pattern you just built.
legacyExercises.passage: Mon collègue Marc, qui est très sympa, m’aide avec le rapport que je dois finir. Nous travaillons dans le bureau où il y a une grande fenêtre. Le jour où nous finirons, nous fêterons ça !
legacyExercises.translation: My colleague Marc, who is very nice, is helping me with the report that I have to finish. We work in the office where there’s a big window. The day we finish, we’ll celebrate !

lessons.culturalNote: Relative pronouns are the architecture of French sentences — long, elegant, linked. English cuts ideas short; French weaves them with qui, que, où into one flowing period.

lessons.title: More, less, as
lessons.objective: Compare with plus/moins/aussi + adjectif + que; note bon → meilleur.

legacyExercises.prompt: Paris est plus grand que Lyon. Which word starts the comparison — “more” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: plus — the “more” marker. grand is the adjective (agreeing with Paris, masculine); que is the “than” hinge; Lyon is just the rival.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: moins + adjective + que. “The train is less expensive.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Le train est moins cher. moins opens it, cher describes the train, and que would introduce the rival if there were one.

legacyExercises.prompt: L’hôtel est aussi beau. Which comparison is this — more, less, or as ?
legacyExercises.explanation: as — aussi + adjective (+ que) means “as … as”. The que is implied here: as beautiful (as the other one).

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “This flight is faster.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Ce vol est plus rapide. plus + rapide, agreeing with vol (masculine) — no que needed when there’s no rival named.

answers: L’avion est plus rapide que le train.
legacyExercises.prompt: Compare with a rival: “The plane is faster than the train.”
legacyExercises.explanation: L’avion est plus rapide que le train. The full sandwich: plus + adjective + que + rival.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Le train est ___ confortable que l’avion.
legacyExercises.explanation: plus — the train wins this round. The sandwich needs its opener: plus/moins/aussi.

legacyExercises.prompt: What does he prefer ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Le train — “the train”. The whole passage is a comparison workout: plus confortable, plus rapide, plus cher, aussi beau.
legacyExercises.passage: Pour voyager, le train est plus confortable que l’avion, mais l’avion est plus rapide. L’hôtel à Paris est plus cher qu’à Lyon, mais il est aussi beau. Moi, je préfère le train !
legacyExercises.translation: For traveling, the train is more comfortable than the plane, but the plane is faster. The hotel in Paris is more expensive than in Lyon, but it’s just as beautiful. Me, I prefer the train !

lessons.culturalNote: Comparisons fuel French café debates — train vs plane, Paris vs Lyon, always with plus and moins flying. And remember the one rebel: bon doesn’t do “plus bon” — it becomes meilleur.

lessons.title: The most, the least, the best
lessons.objective: Build superlatives: le/la/les + plus/moins + adjectif (+ de); use le meilleur / le pire.

legacyExercises.prompt: C’est le plus grand. Which word makes it “the most” — the superlative marker ?
legacyExercises.explanation: plus — but it only becomes “the most” with its crown, le. C’est just presents; grand is the adjective.

legacyExercises.prompt: Think: la + moins + chère (feminine). “It’s the cheapest (hotel).”
legacyExercises.explanation: C’est la moins chère. Feminine crown la, moins for “least”, chère agreeing feminine — the whole agreement chain.

answers: bon is irregular — it becomes meilleur
legacyExercises.prompt: Le meilleur restaurant. Why not “le plus bon” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: bon is irregular — it becomes meilleur. “le plus bon” is the mistake every learner makes once; now you’ll never make it.
options: bon is irregular — it becomes meilleur

legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “The most beautiful view.”
legacyExercises.explanation: La plus belle vue. Feminine crown la, plus, belle agreeing with vue — the full agreement chain in four words.

legacyExercises.prompt: Crown it: “The most famous monument.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Le monument le plus célèbre. Note the word order: with a noun, the crown repeats after it — le monument le plus célèbre.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: C’est ___ restaurant de Paris. (good → best)
legacyExercises.explanation: le meilleur — bon’s irregular crown. “le plus bon” would betray you.

legacyExercises.prompt: What does the Louvre have ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: La plus belle collection — “the most beautiful collection”. The superlative doing its job in the wild.
legacyExercises.passage: Paris est ma ville préférée. La Tour Eiffel est le monument le plus célèbre, et le Louvre a la plus belle collection. Pour moi, c’est le meilleur restaurant de Paris qui a la plus belle vue !
legacyExercises.translation: Paris is my favorite city. The Eiffel Tower is the most famous monument, and the Louvre has the most beautiful collection. For me, it’s the best restaurant in Paris that has the most beautiful view !

lessons.culturalNote: Superlatives are a French art form — le meilleur croissant, la plus belle vue. Every town claims one. Using them well is half the pleasure of recommending anything in France.

lessons.title: Il faut que… (first subjunctive)
lessons.objective: Use il faut que + subjunctive: form it from the ils-present stem (ils -ent + -e/-es/-e/-ions/-iez/-ent).

legacyExercises.prompt: Il faut que tu viennes. Which chunk triggers the subjunctive — “it’s necessary that” ?
legacyExercises.explanation: Il faut que — the trigger. tu viennes is the subjunctive clause it opens; viennes looks like the present, but the que tells you it’s the new mood.

answers: Il faut que tu boives de l’eau.
legacyExercises.prompt: Think: ils boivent → stem boiv- + -e. “You must drink water.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Il faut que tu boives de l’eau. Stem boiv- from the ils present, ending -e for tu — the subjunctive machine working.

legacyExercises.prompt: Il faut qu’elle dorme. The verb after que looks like the present — but what tells you it’s the subjunctive ?
legacyExercises.explanation: the que after il faut — the trigger is the signal. dorme happens to look like the present; the mood comes from il faut que.

answers: Il faut que je me repose.
legacyExercises.prompt: Build it with the blocks: “I need to rest.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Il faut que je me repose. The trigger, then the subjunctive: ils se reposent → stem repos- + -e.

answers: Il faut qu’elle dorme huit heures.
legacyExercises.prompt: Say it: “She must sleep eight hours.”
legacyExercises.explanation: Il faut qu’elle dorme huit heures. qu’elle with élision, then dorme — ils dorment → dorm- + -e.

legacyExercises.prompt: Complete: Il faut que tu ___ ton médicament. (prendre)
legacyExercises.explanation: prennes — ils prennent → prenn- + -es for tu. The double n comes from the ils form, not from nowhere.

legacyExercises.prompt: How many hours must he sleep ? (Reading)
legacyExercises.explanation: Huit heures — “eight hours”. Three il faut que in a row: the doctor’s orders, in the subjunctive.
legacyExercises.passage: Tu es malade ? Il faut que tu te reposes. Il faut que tu boives beaucoup d’eau et il faut que tu dormes huit heures. Le médecin dit qu’il faut que tu prennes ton médicament.
legacyExercises.translation: Are you sick ? You need to rest. You must drink lots of water and you must sleep eight hours. The doctor says you must take your medicine.

lessons.culturalNote: Il faut que is the Swiss-army knife of French necessity — doctors, mothers, and bosses all live in it. Good news: for most verbs the subjunctive looks exactly like the present, so your ear already half-knows it.
